paras: The threatened lynching of John Broadnax occurred in March 1903 in Rockingham County, North Carolina, after Broadnax, a Black youth of sixteen, was accused of killing the farmer Sidney Blair and wounding his niece, Sallie Walker, near Reidsville. Talk of lynching among the neighbors who caught him, and later reports of armed men from Rockingham, led officials to move him to Greensboro and then to Raleigh while National Guard companies stood ready. No attack on him took place; he was convicted at a special term of court and hanged at Wentworth on May 22, 1903.

Blair, about sixty, was a native of Pittsylvania County, Virginia, who had lived in Rockingham County for about ten years, and Walker, about twenty-five, kept his house and taught school in the neighborhood. Broadnax had worked as a farm laborer in the Carmel section, and residents suspected him of an earlier theft of about $60 from Blair's home.

On the evening of Thursday, March 19, Broadnax entered the house while Blair and Walker were at supper, talked with Blair, and then opened fire with a pistol, killing Blair and wounding Walker. Walker's own account, given to a Charlotte Observer correspondent, said he fired at her first; she pushed him out and walked a mile for help. Neighbors found Broadnax in the house pillaging; the dispatches said he surrendered without resistance, while Walker said he tried to escape and stayed only after a guard fired at him.

As word spread, the premises filled with people, and when 'two or three' argued that his confession made his guilt certain, Deputy Sheriff John C. Faucette told them, "I know your faces," and threatened to arrest anyone who harmed him. The warning quieted the crowd, and Faucette and J. D. Glass lodged Broadnax in the Wentworth jail before midnight.

Owing to fear of lynching, he was carried to Greensboro on March 20, while Company G of the Third Regiment was held at its armory under orders to protect him. In Greensboro the authorities obtained Governor Aycock's permission to call out the Gate City Guards, and a correspondent noted that a hundred or more people from Rockingham were in the city, 'waiting in silence'. After the Guilford sheriff reported that an armed body of men was coming from Reidsville to lynch him, the governor ordered Broadnax to Raleigh, and he was woken and put on the midnight train amid a report that another mob was on its way.

Back in Reidsville opinion was divided: many believed he would have been lynched had he stayed in the county jail, while others thought there had been more talk than anything else. The county commissioners drew jurors for the special term that Governor Aycock had ordered for the week of April 13 under Judge B. F. Long.

When Faucette brought Broadnax back from the Wake county jail on April 10, he said there was no thought of lynching in Reidsville, and the News & Observer credited the speedy special term with allaying the desire for lynching. Asked why he had done it, Broadnax answered, "Because Nat Fuller asked me to do it"; no report of any action against Fuller was found. Four lawyers were appointed to defend him, and the jury found him guilty of first-degree murder in fifteen minutes. Sentenced to hang on May 22, he was hanged at Wentworth that day, reportedly expressing contrition for his crime.

The coverage came entirely from white papers, led by the Raleigh News & Observer and the Richmond Times-Dispatch. The Times-Dispatch headlined the 'Prompt Action of the Sheriff in Suppressing a Threatened Lynching' and later 'Lynching Prevented', while both papers called the shooting the darkest crime in the county's annals. The News & Observer approved of the protection yet called Broadnax 'the brute' and wrote that the wires 'were being kept hot to protect him from swift justice'.

A Charlotte Observer dispatch carried the story on March 21 to papers in Virginia, Kentucky, Maine and Texas under headlines such as 'Young Fiend' and 'Deed of a Negro'. A shorter version ran days later in West Virginia and Kansas as 'Narrowly Escaped Lynching' and 'Protecting a Negro from Lynching', and the Lancaster Ledger in South Carolina reported the hanging.

Reports put the shooting on March 19 in the same-day Reidsville dispatches but on March 16, 20 or 22 in later summaries, and gave Broadnax's age as sixteen or fifteen. Walker was first said to have been shot three times, but a Reidsville report two days later said she was wounded in only two places.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of John Broadnax
bases: A threatened lynching: a crowd at the scene talked of lynching the captured Broadnax and was warned off by a deputy, and reports of armed men from Rockingham led officials to move him twice under guard; no attack on him is reported (A1, A2, A7, A8).

Separate Reidsville and Greensboro specials in the News & Observer and Times-Dispatch agree on the lynching talk, the deputy's warning and the removals under guard (A1, A2, A7, A8, A10), though a Reidsville report says opinion was divided on how serious the danger was (A10, A11).

accounts.label: Reidsville correspondent
accounts.gist: Broadnax shot Blair and Walker at supper and was caught pillaging; when 'two or three' at the gathering urged that his guilt was certain, Deputy Faucette threatened to arrest anyone who harmed him, which quieted the crowd.

accounts.label: Sallie Walker's statement
accounts.gist: Walker said Broadnax fired at her first, then at her uncle, and that when neighbors came he tried to escape but stayed in the house after a guard fired at him.

accounts.label: Greensboro correspondent
accounts.gist: A hundred or more Rockingham people were in Greensboro and an armed body was reported coming to lynch him, so troops were called out and the governor had him moved to Raleigh by the midnight train.

accounts.label: Reidsville opinion afterward
accounts.gist: Many thought he would have been lynched had he stayed in the county jail; others thought there was more talk than anything else.

accounts.label: Deputy Faucette, April
accounts.gist: On returning Broadnax for trial, Faucette said there was no thought of lynching in Reidsville and credited the governor's prompt special term.

framing.detail: The Times-Dispatch headlined the 'Prompt Action of the Sheriff in Suppressing a Threatened Lynching' and later 'Lynching Prevented', while calling the crime one of the darkest in the county's annals.
The News & Observer reported the protection approvingly but called Broadnax 'the brute' and wrote of wires 'kept hot to protect him from swift justice', dwelling on his coolness and clothes.
Out-of-state papers ran the Charlotte Observer wire under headlines such as 'Young Fiend', 'Deed of a Negro' and 'Narrowly Escaped Lynching'.

info: Shooting on the evening of Thursday, March 19, 1903, with lynching talk at the scene that night; threats reported in Greensboro March 20; prisoner moved to Raleigh about 1 a.m. March 21
Blair home in the Carmel section, five miles from Reidsville; then Wentworth jail, Greensboro jail and Raleigh (Wake county) jail
John Broadnax, described as a 'negro' boy of sixteen (fifteen in some reports; 'mulatto' in one), threatened with lynching; not harmed
Accused of shooting and killing Sidney (Sydney) Blair, about sixty, and wounding his niece Sallie Walker, in an attempt to rob the house; reported to have confessed
Neighbors who gathered at the Blair home, 'two or three' of whom urged summary action; later, a reported armed body from Reidsville and a hundred or more Rockingham people in Greensboro; none named
Sentenced to hang May 22, 1903, and reported hanged at Wentworth on that date
